content: 1. The implications of providing nutrient supplements and fortified food products, such as multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs), small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS), and fortified cereal-grain-based complementary foods, through public sector programs must be carefully evaluated in terms of their sustainability. This includes assessing the long-term feasibility of such interventions and their integration into existing public health systems. 2. Responsive feeding is a critical component of child nutrition and development. It involves recognizing and responding to a child’s hunger and satiety cues in a timely and appropriate manner. This practice fosters healthy eating behaviors and supports optimal growth and development in children. 3. In specific settings, additional components may be required to enhance the effectiveness of responsive feeding. These could include cultural adaptations, caregiver education, and strategies to address food insecurity or limited access to diverse foods. 4. Practicing responsive feeding has operational implications for caregivers, particularly in terms of the time required for attentive feeding and the potential for food waste. These factors must be considered when designing and implementing responsive feeding interventions. 5. Standardized protocols may be necessary to clearly define the recommended components of responsive feeding, including the duration and intensity of interventions. Such protocols can help ensure consistency and effectiveness in program delivery. 6. The feasibility and costs associated with integrating responsive feeding interventions into healthcare and other settings need to be thoroughly assessed. This includes evaluating the resources required for training, implementation, and monitoring, as well as the potential benefits in terms of improved child health outcomes. 7. The current WHO guideline for complementary feeding of infants and young children aged 6–23 months is available on the WHO website, including the WHO Nutrition website and the WHO e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA). It is also disseminated through a broad network of international partners, including WHO country and regional offices, ministries of health, collaborating centers, universities, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. 8. The WHO steering committee will continue to monitor research developments in complementary feeding, particularly in areas where the certainty of evidence is low or very low. If new evidence warrants an update to the guideline or raises concerns about its validity, the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, in collaboration with other WHO departments or programs, will coordinate the update following the formal procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. 9. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety will conduct a search for new evidence to ensure the recommendations remain relevant and evidence-based.
